content: STAT1, or Signal Transducer and Activator of Transcription 1, is a transcription factor encoded by the STAT1 gene in humans. It belongs to the STAT protein family. Function All STAT proteins are phosphorylated by receptor-associated kinases, which activate them, promote their dimerization (either as homodimers or heterodimers), and facilitate their translocation to the nucleus, where they function as transcription factors. STAT1 can be activated by various ligands, including Interferon-alpha (IFN-α), Interferon-gamma (IFN-γ), Epidermal Growth Factor (EGF), Platelet-Derived Growth Factor (PDGF), and Interleukin-6 (IL-6). Type I interferons (IFN-α and IFN-β) bind to their receptors, triggering signaling cascades via kinases such as TYK2 and JAK1, which phosphorylate and activate STAT1 and STAT2. Activated STAT molecules form dimers and bind to ISGF3G/IRF-9, a component of the Interferon-Stimulated Gene Factor 3 (ISGF3) complex, allowing STAT1 to enter the nucleus. STAT1 plays a critical role in regulating the expression of numerous genes involved in cell survival, viability, and pathogen response. Alternative splicing of the STAT1 gene produces two isoforms of the protein. STAT1 is involved in upregulating genes in response to signals from Type I, Type II, or Type III interferons. Upon stimulation with IFN-γ, STAT1 forms homodimers or heterodimers with STAT3, which bind to the GAS (Gamma-Activated Sequence) promoter element. In response to IFN-α or IFN-β, STAT1 forms heterodimers with STAT2, which bind to the ISRE (Interferon-Stimulated Response Element) promoter element. Binding to these promoter elements increases the expression of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs). STAT1 expression can also be induced by diallyl disulfide, a compound found in garlic. Mutations of STAT1 Mutations in the STAT1 gene can result in either gain-of-function (GOF) or loss-of-function (LOF) alterations, both of which lead to distinct phenotypes and symptoms. Recurrent infections are common in both GOF and LOF mutations. Loss of Function Loss-of-function mutations in STAT1, leading to STAT1 deficiency, can manifest in various forms. Two primary genetic impairments affect responses to Type I and Type III interferons. 1. Autosomal Recessive Deficiency: This can be partial or complete. Partial deficiency is associated with intracellular bacterial diseases or viral infections, along with impaired responses to IFN-α, IFN-β, IFN-γ, and IL-27. High levels of IFN-γ may be detected in the blood serum in partial deficiency. Monocytes from whole blood fail to respond to BCG and IFN-γ stimulation with IL-12 production. Complete recessive deficiency results in a severely diminished response to antiviral and antifungal medications. 2. Autosomal Dominant Partial Deficiency: This form is characterized by impaired IFN-γ responses and selective susceptibility to intracellular bacterial diseases, such as Mendelian Susceptibility to Mycobacterial Disease (MSMD). Knockout mice studies in the 1990s revealed reduced CD4+ and CD25+ regulatory T cells and an almost complete lack of IFN-α, IFN-β, and IFN-γ responses, leading to parasitic, viral, and bacterial infections. The first reported case of STAT1 deficiency in humans involved an autosomal dominant mutation, with patients showing susceptibility to mycobacterial infections. Another case involved an autosomal recessive form, where two related patients had a homozygous missense STAT1 mutation causing defective splicing and impaired mature protein function. These patients exhibited a partially compromised response to both IFN-α and IFN-γ. Recessive STAT1 deficiency is now recognized as a novel form of primary immunodeficiency. Patients presenting with sudden, severe, and unexpected bacterial or viral infections should be evaluated for potential STAT1 deficiency. Gain of Function Gain-of-function mutations in STAT1 were first identified in patients with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (CMC). This condition is characterized by persistent infections of the skin, mucosae (oral or genital), and nails caused by Candida species, primarily Candida albicans. CMC is often associated with primary immunodeficiency. Patients with CMC frequently experience bacterial infections (commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus), respiratory tract infections, and skin infections. Viral infections, particularly those caused by Herpesviridae, are also common and often affect the skin. Mycobacterial infections, typically caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis or environmental bacteria, are also observed. Autoimmune symptoms, such as Type 1 diabetes, cytopenia, thymic regression, or systemic lupus erythematosus, are frequently reported in these patients. Autoimmune diseases are particularly common in individuals with T-cell deficiencies. CMC is also a common symptom in patients with hyperimmunoglobulin E syndrome (hyper-IgE) and autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type I. A role for interleukin-17A (IL-17A) has been identified in CMC, as low levels of IL-17A-producing T cells are observed in affected patients. Genomic and genetic studies have revealed that a heterozygous gain-of-function mutation in STAT1 accounts for more than half of CMC cases. These mutations often occur in the coiled-coil domain, DNA-binding domain, N-terminal domain, or SH2 domain of STAT1. The mutations result in increased phosphorylation due to defective dephosphorylation in the nucleus. These processes are dependent on cytokines such as IFN-α, IFN-β, IFN-γ, and IL-27. Impaired Th17 polarization of the immune response, due to low IL-17A levels, is a hallmark of STAT1 GOF mutations. Patients with STAT1 GOF mutations and CMC often respond poorly or not at all to treatment with azole antifungal drugs, such as fluconazole, itraconazole, or posaconazole. In addition to common viral and bacterial infections, these patients may develop autoimmune diseases or even carcinomas. Treatment is challenging due to the wide range of symptoms and drug resistances. JAK/STAT pathway inhibitors, such as ruxolitinib, are currently being tested as potential therapeutic options for these patients. Interactions STAT1 has been shown to interact with several proteins, including: BRCA1 C-jun CD117 CREB-binding protein Calcitriol receptor Epidermal growth factor receptor Fanconi anemia, complementation group C GNB2L1 IFNAR2 IRF1 ISGF3G Interleukin-27 receptor, alpha subunit MCM5 Mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) PIAS1 PRKCD PTK2 Protein kinase R STAT2 STAT3 Src TRADD
